The Württemberg *Familienregister* recorded each household as a named unit on one page or spread: father, mother with maiden name, and all children with baptism dates listed together. A single entry can hand you both parents and every sibling at once — the highest-yield first move for a Württemberg parentage question.

**What to look for:** Open the Familienregister volume(s) on the Archion page above and browse for any entry under the surname **Seeger**. Note the father's full name, the mother's full name and maiden name, and any children listed (especially one named Katharina born c. 1843).

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn (b. ca. 1845) would be approximately 25 in 1870 — possibly establishing his own household or still residing with Thomas Flynn (~50–60 if Thomas is the father). United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable (personCount 38558371). A household entry placing Patrick with Thomas would directly corroborate the parent-child link established from the 1850 and 1860 census searches (pl_001, pl_002). Even if Patrick heads his own household, the entry pins his adult residence and narrows the search for Thomas independently. Search 'Flynn' spelling variants (Flinn, Flyn) if the primary spelling yields nothing.

Ancestry holds an independent transcription of the 1870 US census with its own name index. Transcription variants ('Flinn', 'Flyn') present in the FamilySearch index may differ from Ancestry's, and vice versa. Search Ancestry only if pli_006 (FamilySearch 1870) yields nothing useful in Schuylkill County.

Patrick Flynn (~35) and Thomas Flynn (~65, if still living) are both plausible 1880 enumerees. United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable (personCount 50169452) and uniquely records each person's relationship to the head of household — if Thomas resides with Patrick, the relationship column would explicitly name him (e.g., 'Father'), providing the strongest direct documentary link of any census year. The 1880 schedule also records each person's own birthplace and parents' birthplaces, which may confirm or extend what the death certificate recorded. Note: the 1890 census schedules were largely destroyed in a 1921 fire and cannot bridge this decade.

Ancestry's independent transcription of the 1880 census as a fallback. The 1880 relationship column is the highest-value field for this question, so a surname transcription error in the FamilySearch index that buries the household warrants a cross-check. Search Ancestry only if pli_008 (FamilySearch 1880) yields nothing in Schuylkill County.

Patrick Flynn (~55) would be an established head of household in 1900 — the last census before his 1908 death. Thomas Flynn, if alive, would be approximately 80–90 and might appear in Patrick's household as a widowed parent; even his absence is informative. United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable (personCount 76211837) and records each person's parents' birthplaces, which may confirm or supplement the parental origin evidence from the death certificate already searched in pl_002.
Ancestry's independent transcription of the 1900 census as a fallback. Search only if pli_010 (FamilySearch 1900) yields nothing for Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County.

## Research Plan — pl_002

**Context:** The current proof summary (ps_001) sits at tier **"Possible / gap"** — the only supporting evidence is the 1850 census co-enumeration of Patrick with Thomas Flynn (indirect, inferred). The mother is entirely unknown. Nine searches remain.

---

### Execution order

|---|-------------|--------|--------|---------------|
| 1 (pli_004) | **1860 US Federal Census** | FamilySearch | 1860 | name-searchable (personCount 27,518,891) |
| 2 (pli_005) | **Patrick's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate** | FamilySearch | 1908 | name-searchable |
| 3 (pli_006) | **Schuylkill Co. church records — Patrick's burial/confirmation** | FamilySearch (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) | 1845–1908 | name-searchable (personCount 982,415) |
| 4 (pli_007) | **Thomas Flynn & wife marriage record** | FamilySearch (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) | 1835–1860 | name-searchable (personCount 982,415) |
| 5 (pli_008) | **Thomas Flynn probate / will** | FamilySearch (browse) | 1851–1910 | browse-only (personCount 0) — vol. 007936749 |
| 6 (pli_009) | **1870 US Federal Census** | FamilySearch | 1870 | name-searchable (personCount 38,558,371) |
| 7 (pli_010) | **Patrick's marriage record (FAN)** | FamilySearch | 1865–1895 | SYNTH-PA-CHURCH name-searchable; vol. 007936753 browse-only |
| 8 (pli_011) | **Thomas Flynn naturalization** | FamilySearch (browse) | 1849–1880 | browse-only (personCount 0) — vol. 007936750 |
| 9 (pli_012) | **Ancestry 1860 census** *(fallback for #1)* | Ancestry | 1860 | name-searchable |

---

### Rationale highlights

**Item 1 — 1860 census:** Patrick (~15) is almost certainly still in Thomas's household. A second co-enumeration under the same surname strengthens the inferred child relationship. Crucially, any woman in the household is a candidate mother — her name and age drive items 4 and 5. Search Flinn and Flyn variants.

**Item 2 — 1908 death certificate:** Pennsylvania civil registration began 1906 (loc_001). The informant may name *both* parents, giving the first documentary evidence of the mother's name and maiden name. Also likely to record Patrick's Irish origin town, unlocking Irish record research. Since Patrick's birth parish is unknown, this is one of the primary records expected to state a birthplace — per the guidance that unknown birth parishes require planning the subject's own death entry as its own item.

**Item 3 — Church records (burial/confirmation):** SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable across all Schuylkill County parishes (1708–1985). A baptism in Ireland is unlikely to appear here, but the 1908 burial entry in a local Catholic register routinely states age, birthplace, and sometimes parents. RC registers fall under the Diocese of Scranton (post-1868) per loc_001.

**Item 4 — Parents' marriage:** Required for every parentage plan. Confirms Thomas and wife as a unit, supplies the mother's maiden name (if her first marriage), and corroborates Thomas as father by date. **Caution:** marriage likely occurred in Ireland before ~1845 and may not appear in Pennsylvania records — absence here would redirect research to Irish registers.

**Item 5 — Thomas Flynn probate:** The Schuylkill County Register of Wills holds probate from 1811 (loc_001). A will naming Patrick as a son is *direct* evidence of parentage. The date window (1851–1910) is set by Thomas's plausible lifespan as the father of a child born in 1845 — not by Patrick's own research window.

**Item 6 — 1870 census:** Locates Thomas if still alive (~50–60 by then), narrows the probate date window (item 5), and confirms the family's continued Schuylkill County residence.

**Item 7 — Patrick's marriage record (FAN):** Pennsylvania marriage records often name the groom's father. Witnesses are typically family members whose testimony about Patrick's parentage may appear in the record. This is the required FAN item for a parentage question.

**Item 8 — Thomas Flynn naturalization:** If Thomas naturalized in Schuylkill County (vol. 007936750, 1849–1915), his petition may name his wife, children, and Irish place of origin — potentially identifying the specific parish.

**Item 9 — Ancestry 1860 census (fallback for #1):** Independent indexing may capture Flinn/Flyn spellings or correct transcription errors if FamilySearch yields nothing.

- If item **1** (FamilySearch 1860) finds nothing → search item **9** (Ancestry 1860)

entry.rationale: The 1860 US Federal Census (collection 1473181) is name-searchable (personCount 27,518,891). Patrick would be ~15 in 1860 and very likely still resident in Thomas Flynn's household. A second consecutive co-enumeration of Patrick with Thomas under the same surname strengthens the inferred child relationship established from the 1850 census (a_004). Also note any woman in the household who could be Patrick's mother — her name and age would directly inform the marriage and church record searches that follow. Search variant spellings Flinn and Flyn.

Pennsylvania civil death registration began 1906 (loc_001 quirks); Patrick Flynn died in 1908 in Schuylkill County, so a state death certificate exists. The informant — often a child or surviving spouse — may name both of Patrick's parents, providing the only documentary evidence of the mother's name and maiden name. The birthplace field may also record Patrick's Irish origin town, which would unlock Irish church record searches. Additionally, since Patrick's birth parish is unknown (he was born in Ireland ~1845 and the parish is the unknown being sought), this death entry is one of the primary records expected to state an age and place of origin. Highest-value item for identifying both parents.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415) and covers 1708–1985. Patrick's birth parish is unknown (born Ireland ~1845, emigrated as a young child), so a baptism record is unlikely to appear here. However, his 1908 burial entry in a local Catholic parish register — typical for the anthracite coal region's Irish immigrant community — routinely states age, birthplace, and sometimes parents' names. Also search for a confirmation or membership record entered upon the family's arrival in the 1840s–1850s. Because the birth parish is unknown, the death/burial entry is the primary target in this collection. The loc_001 locality guide notes RC parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868 and the Diocese of Scranton thereafter; registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county courthouse.

A dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other is required for every parentage plan. The marriage record (a) confirms Thomas Flynn and his wife as a unit; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name — absent from census and most death records — provided this was her first marriage; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth corroborates Thomas as father. Search SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable (personCount 982,415), for a Thomas Flynn marriage in Schuylkill County. Note: the couple likely married in Ireland before emigrating ca. 1845; if no Pennsylvania record is found, the marriage predates arrival and will require separate Irish record research. Volume 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records 1842–1895, browse-only, personCount 0) is available as an image-browse fallback. The marriage record confirms the couple married — it does not, by itself, establish that Patrick is their child; a record placing Patrick with the parents (census household, baptism, or probate) is still needed for that link.

Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); the loc_001 locality guide confirms the Schuylkill County Register of Wills holds probate from 1811 and that this is a primary parentage source naming heirs. The county-specific volume 007936749 (Schuylkill Probate Records 1851–1930) is also browse-only (personCount 0). If Thomas Flynn left a will naming Patrick as a son, that is direct evidence of the father-son relationship; the will may also name Thomas's wife and other children, corroborating the family structure and identifying the mother. Thomas's death date is unknown; as the father of a child born in 1845, Thomas was likely born ca. 1810–1825, so his death could fall anywhere from the early 1850s to ca. 1910. The date window is set by Thomas's plausible lifespan, not by Patrick's research window.

The 1870 US Federal Census (collection 1438024) is name-searchable (personCount 38,558,371). Patrick would be ~25 in 1870; Thomas, if still alive, would be ~50–60. Finding both in the same household or the same county further corroborates the parent-child relationship and, if Thomas remains the head, confirms the family unit persisted. Even if Patrick has formed his own household, locating Thomas narrows the probate search window (item 5). The birthplace column for Thomas — if it reads Ireland — aligns with Patrick's 1850 entry and reinforces that the correct Thomas Flynn family has been identified.

Patrick's own marriage record (if he married in Pennsylvania) often names the groom's father and may name both parents; witnesses are typically family members or close associates who could corroborate the Flynn–Thomas connection and help identify the mother. This is the required FAN item for a parentage question: the spouse, witnesses, and officiants are associates whose testimony about Patrick's parentage may appear in the record. Volume 007936753 (Schuylkill County Marriage Records 1870–1910) is browse-only (personCount 0); SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (name-searchable, personCount 982,415) may also hold the church marriage register entry. Patrick born ~1845 would have married roughly 1865–1895.

Volume 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849–1915) is browse-only (personCount 0). If Thomas Flynn naturalized in Schuylkill County, his petition or declaration of intention may name his wife, children, and place of origin in Ireland — evidence that would both corroborate the family structure and potentially identify the specific Irish parish from which to seek baptism records. Browse for Thomas Flynn in the 1849–1880 window: a man who arrived ca. 1845–1850 would most likely have naturalized within the following 20–30 years.

Ancestry maintains an independent index of the 1860 census that may capture variant spellings (Flinn, Flyn) or correct transcription errors missed by the FamilySearch index. Search here if item pli_004 (FamilySearch 1860 census) yields no Patrick or Thomas Flynn match in Schuylkill County.

### Step 1 — `pli_001` · 1860 U.S. Census, Blount County, Alabama · FamilySearch
Verify the tree lead before building on it. Collection 1927240 "United States Census (Population Schedules), 1860" — **name-searchable (personCount 23,000,000)**; volume 005154190 — 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable (loc_001). Search "Wood" and variant "Woods." If a Wood household with a girl ~age 1 is confirmed, the head and co-resident adults become the leading candidate parents.

### Step 2 — `pli_002` · 1880 U.S. Census, Hill County, Texas · FamilySearch
Martha married James M Neal in Hill County on 31 Jul 1879 and should appear there in 1880 as "Martha Neal," age ~21. The 1880 Federal Census uniquely records the **father's birthplace and mother's birthplace** for every person enumerated — those two fields directly narrow which state (or region) to prioritize, independent of the Alabama lead.

---

### Step 3 — `pli_003` · Blount County, Alabama marriage records, 1855–1868 · FamilySearch
Test whether "Wood" is Martha's birth surname or a prior married name. Search for any bride named "M J Wood," "Martha Wood," or "Martha J Wood" in collection 1598408 "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" — **name-searchable (personCount 1,224,690)**; volume 007316662 (92% name-indexed, full-text searchable). If a match surfaces, the plan must pivot away from the "Wood" birth-family hypothesis.

### Step 4 — `pli_004` · Blount County, Alabama marriage records, 1840–1858 · FamilySearch
Dedicated plan item for the **candidate parents' marriage to each other**. A Wood-surname marriage in Blount County before Martha's birth (~1859) would supply the mother's maiden name (census and death records omit it), confirm the couple as a unit, and by date corroborate any father named only by the 1860 census. Note: their marriage alone does not prove Martha is their child — item 1 must place her with them. Also search "Woods." Same collection and volume as item 3.

---

### Step 5 — `pli_005` · 1870 U.S. Census, Blount County, Alabama + Smith County, Texas · FamilySearch
Martha left Alabama by January 1869. Wood family members who stayed in Alabama appear in 1870 Blount County as a surviving parental or sibling household; those who followed her appear in 1870 Smith County, Texas. Search both jurisdictions (and Hill County, Texas as a secondary). Supplies parents' or siblings' names and ages.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.
Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: US federal censuses enumerate all household members by name, age, and birthplace. Searching United States Census 1860 (collection 1473181, name-searchable, personCount 27,518,891), 1870 (collection 1438024, name-searchable, personCount 38,558,371), and 1880 (collection 1417683, name-searchable, personCount 50,169,452) for John and Bridget Doyle in Schuylkill County will identify all children present in the household at each enumeration point. The 1880 census adds a relationship-to-head field, making household membership explicit. This three-decade block is the highest-yield starting point for a completeness question: children born in the 1840s–1860s should appear in at least one of these snapshots while still at home. Variant spellings (Doile, Doyell, Doyal) should be tried.

No FamilySearch 1850 census collection was returned by this session's collections_search; the external_links_search returned a dedicated Ancestry collection for the 1850 United States Federal Census, Schuylkill County (ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/). The 1850 census lists free individuals by name and age but does not state family relationships, so children are inferred by age and surname in the Doyle household.

The 1900 US Federal Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable, personCount 76,211,837) asks each married woman how many children she has borne and how many are still living — a direct completeness check if Bridget survived to 1900. Adult Doyle children who left the parental household would appear in their own 1900 Schuylkill County (or adjacent county) households, searchable by the Doyle surname. Searching on 'Doyle' across Schuylkill County will surface children who remained in the region even after leaving the parental home.

Irish Catholic Doyle children would have been baptized at the local Roman Catholic parish — under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868, then the Diocese of Scranton (per loc_001 quirk). A name search for 'Doyle' with parents 'John' and 'Bridget'/'Halloran' will surface each baptism record naming the child, parents, and date. This is the single record type most likely to enumerate every child individually. Variant spellings (Doile, Doyell) and first-name variants should be tried.

John Doyle's will or estate administration would name his heirs — typically all living children at the time of his death. Date window 1845–1905 is set by John's plausible lifespan as the creator of this record — he was active in the coal region from at least the 1840s and likely died before Bridget's remarriage. A probate naming all children would be near-conclusive for the completeness question.

The Schuylkill County marriage records image volume (007936753, browse-only, personCount 0; dates 1870–1910) covers the period when Doyle children of marrying age would have wed in the county. Daughters would appear under the Doyle surname as brides; sons as grooms. Marriage entries in this era sometimes state the bride's or groom's parents by name, corroborating parentage. Browsing for 'Doyle' marriages will surface adult children not yet captured in household census records or baptism registers. Note that PA statewide civil registration did not begin until 1906 (loc_001 quirk), so this volume represents county-level marriage licensing records, not state vital registration.

Fallback for the indexed church baptism search (pli_004). Per loc_001 quirks, some church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups. If the indexed search (pli_004) misses baptisms not yet indexed, browsing the Catholic parish registers page by page for the years 1840–1875 will identify Doyle children whose baptism records were not captured by the index.

FAN item: John Doyle's naturalization papers (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, volume 007936750, browse-only, personCount 0; dates 1849–1915) may list his spouse and children — declarations of intent and first papers in this era sometimes recorded family composition. As an Irish immigrant in the anthracite coal region, John Doyle would likely have naturalized through Schuylkill County courts. A declaration naming his children would corroborate or extend what the census and baptism records show. Date window set to 1849–1900, covering John's plausible naturalization window as the creator of this record.
